extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners and attorneys practicing before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, rules, and sanctioning guidance governing attorneys practicing trademark matters before the USPTO, focusing on signature requirements, supervisory duties over non-practitioner assistants, and related professional conduct violations and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rule (named signatory must sign)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO trademark signature rules require the named signatory to enter his or her signature on a trademark document to be presented to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order emphasizes that this is a substantive rule, not a mere technical requirement; a failure of the named signatory to enter his or her signature may actually or potentially harm applicants' and registrants' intellectual property rights and the integrity of the USPTO trademark registration process. TMEP § 611.01 provides guidance concerning that only the named signatory should enter his or her signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — Competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation to a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent representation includes adequately understanding USPTO trademark signature rules and TMEP guidance. Presenting trademark documents (including declarations) that violate the USPTO trademark signature rules constitutes a violation of § 11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are required to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to ensure compliance with USPTO signature rules (e.g., allowing improperly signed submissions) can violate the duty of diligence and promptness. The Office considers whether the practitioner took timely steps to prevent or correct improper filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b) — Supervisory responsibilities over non-practitioner assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner having direct supervisory authority over a non-practitioner assistant must make reasonable efforts to ensure the non-practitioner's conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner supervises non-attorney trademark assistants, the practitioner must ensure those assistants comply with USPTO rules (including signature requirements). Permitting or directing non-practitioners to enter signatures inconsistent with the named signatory rule breaches this supervisory obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Misrepresentation (presentation of improperly signed documents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in misrepresentation by presenting documents where the practitioner knew the named signatory had not signed the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting trademark documents (including declarations) to the USPTO while knowing the named signatory had not signed them implicates § 11.804(c). The Final Order cites presenting approximately 467 such documents as an example of this misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — Conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the trademark registration system
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that is prejudicial to the integrity of the U.S. trademark registration system, such as presenting improperly signed documents the Office relies upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting improperly signed filings that the USPTO uses in its registration process can be treated as conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the system under § 11.804(d). The Office treats such conduct as more than technical error because of potential adverse effects on IP rights and the registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP § 611.01 guidance on signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP) direction that the named signatory is the person who enters his or her signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are expected to know and follow TMEP guidance. Lack of understanding of TMEP § 611.01 is not an excuse; the TMEP is published and regularly updated and provides practices and procedures for prosecution of trademark applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to remediate and notify clients upon discovering improper filings
rubrics_metrics.description: When violations (e.g., impermissible signatures) are discovered, the practitioner should promptly communicate with affected clients and take corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent directly contacted affected clients, informed them of the impermissible signatures, agreed to take action at no charge, and worked to address any actual or potential harm to clients' intellectual property rights. Timely, candid communication and remediation are mitigating factors in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation and candor with OED investigations as mitigating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Full cooperation with Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) investigations, including candid responses and interviews, is a favorable consideration in resolving disciplinary matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order notes Respondent's full cooperation and candid engagement with OED as an additional consideration supporting the agreed-upon sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of contrition and acknowledgment of harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression of contrition and acknowledgment of the seriousness and potential harm resulting from violations may mitigate sanction severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's contrition and recognition that signature rule failures may harm clients and the registration process were cited as considerations in the settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions available and imposed (public reprimand, probation, suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary outcomes can include public reprimand, probation (e.g., twelve months), and suspension (up to four months) for continued or unremedied violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this matter the agreed sanction was a public reprimand and 12 months' probation while remaining in active good standing; the OED Director may seek suspension (up to four months) via an Order to Show Cause if the practitioner fails to comply with probation terms or the Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation enforcement procedure (Order to Show Cause; 15-day response; referral for suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED believes the practitioner violated probation or the Agreement, OED will issue an Order to Show Cause, allow 15 days for response, and may request the USPTO Director to impose immediate suspension if noncompliance persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order describes the steps: issuance and service of an Order to Show Cause, 15-day response window, submission of record and evidence to the USPTO Director, and request for suspension. Review by practitioner does not postpone any suspension imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of disciplinary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Orders and disciplinary notices will be published electronically in OED's FOIA Reading Room and in the Official Gazette with a notice materially consistent with the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will publish a public reprimand notice describing the misconduct, the sanction, and relevant factual findings; disciplinary decisions are posted for public reading at the OED Reading Room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary record in future proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing prevents the Office from considering this Final Order in future complaints or disciplinary proceedings as an aggravating factor or to rebut statements by the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record of this proceeding may be used (1) when addressing any further complaint or similar misconduct, and/or (2) in any future disciplinary proceeding against Respondent as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations by Respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of procedural rights in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of a settlement, a practitioner may waive rights to seek reconsideration or review under 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.56 and 11.57 and waive other appeals or challenges to the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order records Respondent's waiver of rights to seek reconsideration or review and to otherwise appeal, which is a common term in negotiated disciplinary settlements.
